opener.heading: Week 38: Colors & Shapes Studio 🎨
about: Color and shape arrive this week as materials she works with rather than words she recites. She colors a grid, then fills the real one with cut paper, judges the bluest thing in the house and pins a rosette on it, mixes paint one drop at a time until it matches, prints a border along a strip of paper, threads dyed pasta in a run of three. The repeat is the spine of all of it. A unit starts, runs, breaks somewhere in the middle, and she is the one who finds where.

Thursday is the autumn equinox. Day and night run the same length, and from Friday the dark takes a little more every week until a few days before Christmas, so say it out loud on the walk. That day starts on a circle of leaves and buckeyes laid out on the path, photographed, then swept into a bucket, and ends with the patio chalked and washed off again. Morocco carries Friday's sidebar with its zellij tilework, and Monday's afternoon comes off the back of it: the tray out of the fridge onto a low table, everybody on the floor round it, oranges and cinnamon in the middle.
azlyn: Making a plan and then following it. She colors a grid at 8:00 and works from it at 9:15, which is an hour of holding an intention.
Mixing a color until it matches. White lightens, a touch of black darkens, and blue with yellow in it turns green in front of her.
A pattern that repeats in threes. Square, triangle, circle printed along a strip, and three colors of pasta threaded in the same order.
Reading a room from above. She walks the walls of the downstairs counting corners, then finds each room again on a plan she colored in.
Symmetry, found by folding. One fold, one cut, and the shape comes out twice without anybody using the word.
you: Planning before doing is a real developmental leap
Deciding what deserves recognition is more advanced than receiving it
A map is an abstraction she has to be taught to read
Food is the most memorable route into a culture at this age
Symmetry through folding is discovered, not explained
Repeating units are a genuine step up from alternating patterns
Impermanence is easier to accept when it's built into the design
shopping: One large delivery box, big enough for a flat panel and four squares
Two large sheets of paper for the floor plan, or butcher paper
Magazines, junk mail and packaging for colored paper, 15–20 sheets
Crayons, including a fat one and a red one
Washable non-toxic poster paint in red, blue, yellow, white and black
A wide brush and a smaller one
A glass jar for the brush water
Ribbon, wool, or a grocery bag to cut into strips
A ball of wool or thick string
An old shirt or an apron
An old towel for the back door
A tray or shallow box for the paper scraps
The biggest tray or plate in the house
A basket for collecting, and a bag for the blackberries
Plastic milk-jug caps and jar lids, too wide for his mouth, saved through the week
Cushions or folded blankets, one per person
A basket or bag for each bedroom
A load of laundry run and dried by Tuesday morning
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 15 months this week. He runs, spoons his own food, and points at pictures in books waiting for you to name what he lands on.

days.title: The Tile She Plans First
days.prepTonight: Cut a delivery box into one flat panel and four squares a hand span across, and leave them out with the glue stick, the magazines and a sheet of paper ruled into big squares.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Plan on the Grid Paper

opening.title: The Plan on the Grid Paper
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper ruled into big squares · crayons in 4 or 5 colors · 1 pencil.
steps: Sit down with the ruled sheet and tell her the squares become paper tiles at 9:15, one color each.
She colors them in, in whatever order she takes them. Say the color back as she picks each crayon up.
Write PLAN across the top in pencil and stand it against the wall. She follows this at 9:15, so leave it as it is.

main.title: The Paper Tile Wall
materials: 1 large flat sheet of card, a cereal box or a delivery box cut open
Colored paper: magazine pages, junk mail, cereal boxes, 15–20 sheets
1 glue stick, or masking tape if the glue is dry
steps: Rule the panel into squares with the pencil, the same number across and down as her plan. A hand span each.
Sort the colored paper into piles by color. Cereal boxes do not tear, so cut those with the adult scissors while she works the soft paper with the child-safe pair.
Read the plan a row at a time, top left first. She names the color, goes to that pile and cuts a square.
Glue each one down as it is cut. Cut twenty first and she loses track of where they go.
Halfway along, hold the panel beside the plan and let her check her own work. Masking tape moves anything she wants moved.
Tape the panel to the wall at her eye height once the glue is dry.
main.tip: Her squares will not be square. Glue the wonky ones down untrimmed.

outside.title: The First Turned Leaves
paras: Mid-September and the turn has started at the edges. Walk the road you always walk and hunt for the first leaf that has gone over: a horse chestnut browning at the tips, one red leaf in a green cherry, brambles going purple along a wall. Give her a bag and ask for four leaves in four colors, and stop for the one that is half green and half yellow.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and runs, so the walk goes at his pace or he rides and gets let out at the wall. He points and waits for you to name things. Hold a yellow leaf and a green one up side by side and say both colors. He grabs for one.

second.title: Four Tiles That Turn
second.intro: The four card squares match the ones on the panel and each gets the same design. Turning them makes the pattern.
materials: 4 squares of card, a hand span across, cut from a box
Crayons, or 3 colors of washable poster paint
1 damp washcloth in a shallow bowl
steps: Lay the four squares out and draw the same design on each with the marker: a line corner to opposite corner, a quarter circle in a second corner. All four the same way up.

She fills the shapes in with crayons, or paint and the wide brush. The turning only works if the four match, so say that out loud and hand her the same color each time. Two matching out of four still turns into something.
Wipe her hands on the damp washcloth and lay the four in a two-by-two block, still the same way up.
Turn one square a quarter turn. Look again. Turn a second one.
Keep going until the lines meet across the middle and make a shape none of the four has alone.
Ask her to stop at the one she likes best, then let her turn them at random.
Leave the four out overnight. She will rearrange them before breakfast.
second.tip: Say "a quarter turn" and turn it with her hand under yours, every time. The words arrive attached to the movement.

alternatives: Color a fresh grid plan and change every color.
Cut squares, glue them anywhere on the panel, stop there.
Sort the offcuts into color piles and count each pile.
Lay the four tiles on the floor and walk round them instead.
outAgain: Playgroup, and take the four tiles in a bag to show
The park, where the far end is already under leaves
A friend's house, if anyone can face two under four
The café with the wide window and a hot drink you finish
A slow walk to the mailbox with something to post

aroundWorld.title: Morocco, Zellij Tilework 🔷
paras: In Morocco, craftsmen chip glazed tiles into small shapes by hand and set them into patterns that cover whole walls, fountains and floors. The work is called zellij, and there is no picture in the middle of it: stars, crosses and eight-pointed rosettes repeat out to the edge. A master cutter, a maallem, learns the shapes from another cutter and works with nothing printed in front of him.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Msemen, the square Moroccan pancake, gets folded into quarters before it hits the pan. Let Azlyn do the folding and eat them with honey.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: A zellij pattern has no beginning and no end. It stops only where the wall does.

days.krestonPM: Give him a fat crayon and a magazine page off the sorting piles. At 15 months he scribbles with his whole arm and half of it lands off the paper. He points at pictures in books now, so hold him up to the panel on the wall and name whatever he lands on.

insight.headline: Planning before doing is a real developmental leap.
paras: Azlyn drew the grid at 8:00 and followed it at 9:15, and the hour in between is where the work happened. Holding a plan across an hour and then acting on it runs on her frontal lobes, the slowest part of her brain to build, and three is when it comes online. Most of what she makes still gets invented in her hands as she goes. Following a plan she made earlier is the harder job, because it means overriding whatever the moment suggests. She will break her own plan today, and that counts too, because breaking it means she saw the difference.

days.safety: The adult scissors cut the cereal boxes and nothing else, and they go back in your pocket between cuts. Small cut paper shapes go straight in Kreston's mouth at 15 months, so the offcuts land in one box and the floor gets swept before he is down on it.

days.title: The Color Show
days.prepTonight: Cut six or eight circles the size of a jar lid out of a cereal box and put them out with the clothespins, the ribbon and the felt tips.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Best Blue in the House

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Best Door on the Street

opening.title: Making the Rosettes First
opening.need: the cut paper circles, 6–8 · crayons or felt tips · ribbon or wool · 6–8 clothespins · 1 permanent marker.
steps: Hand her the circles and let her decorate them. They are prizes, and a prize should look like one.
Lay two lengths of ribbon down the back of each circle and clip a peg over both.
Write BEST BLUE, BEST RED and BEST YELLOW on three of them in marker while she watches. The rest stay blank.

main.title: The Best Blue in the House
materials: Paper circles cut from a cereal box, 6–8, decorated this morning
Ribbon, wool or strips of a grocery bag
Whatever is already in the house, in blue, red and yellow
steps: Send her round the downstairs for every blue thing she can carry. Stop her at ten so lunch still happens.
Line them up on the floor in one long row. Stand back and look at it before either of you says anything.
Ask which one is the bluest. Take the answer, then ask why, and sit through the pause.
Clip the BEST BLUE rosette onto the winner so the ribbon hangs down the front, and stand it on the windowsill on its own.
Do red, then yellow, the same way. She gets faster and her reasons get longer.
Give her a blank circle and the felt tips and let her invent a fourth category. Write her words on it in marker and hand her the last of the ribbon.
main.tip: Do not overrule her winner. A navy sock beating a sky-blue cup is a decision about what blue means to her.

outside.title: The Best Door on the Street
paras: Write BEST RED DOOR on one blank circle and BEST BLUE DOOR on another before you go, then judge the street. Walk one side and stop where she stops. Doors come in colors nobody would put on a wall: mailbox red, sage green, a black gloss that holds the sky in it. Let her pick a winner for each, and hold a rosette up from the sidewalk for each one without going up anybody's path.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and points at everything he wants named. Doors sit at his height and each one is a single flat color, easier for him than anything in the house. Say the color every time he points, and nothing else. He will not say them back for months and he is filing them the whole time.

second.title: Matching the Blue Exactly
second.intro: The winning blue thing comes off the windowsill onto the table, and she makes its color on a saucer.
materials: Washable poster paint in red, blue, yellow, white and black
steps: Put a blob of blue on a saucer and paint a patch near the top of a sheet. Hold it against the winning object. It is wrong, and she sees that first.
Ask her whether it has to go lighter or darker. Take her word for it.
Add white for lighter, a touch of black for darker, one small amount at a time, and let her stir. Paint a fresh patch under the last after every change.
Once the ladder of patches runs down the sheet, hold it against the object and let her put a finger on the closest one.
Wash the brush in the jar, dry it on the washcloth, and start a fresh saucer with a drop of red in the blue. Purple arrives, and she did not predict it.
Third saucer, a drop of yellow into blue. Green comes out of two colors that look nothing like it, and she will want it again.
Stand the best-matching sheet beside the object overnight.
second.tip: One drop at a time, and stir before she judges it. Paint moves further than she expects, and a saucer that has gone too far cannot come back.

alternatives: Paint one sheet in every shade of blue she can make.
Sort the house's blue things into light, middle and dark rows.
Mix food coloring in jars of water instead of paint.
Hand the blank rosettes out to people rather than things.
outAgain: A train ride, two stops out and two back, for the ride and nothing else
The station on its own, if the trains are enough
The big park with the rosettes, judging trees
The pet store, and count the colors in the fish tanks
Home early, if the paint ran the full ninety minutes
days.krestonPM: On the train sit him at the window facing forward. At 15 months a moving window holds him longer than anything in the diaper bag, and he points at things too far off to identify. Say something anyway. He runs everywhere now, so the platform is a hand-holding job from the barrier to the seat.

insight.headline: Deciding what deserves recognition is more advanced than receiving it.
paras: Azlyn has been handed stickers and well-dones her whole life. This morning she handed them out, and that runs a different set of muscles. Picking a winner means holding several things in mind at once, weighing them against a standard she had to invent, then defending the choice out loud when you ask why. Children who get to judge rather than be judged are practicing the reasoning that turns up later as an argument with evidence in it. Her reasons will be poor at first. Ask anyway, take whatever comes, and put the rosette where she says it goes rather than where you would have put it.

days.safety: Cut the ribbon and the wool into short lengths and pick up what falls the moment the rosettes are clipped. Pegs and small paper circles stay off the floor while Kreston is down, because he runs everywhere now and both fit in his mouth. The permanent marker goes back capped and out of reach. Washable non-toxic paint only this afternoon, and the water jar stays at the back of the table where he cannot reach in and pull it over.

days.title: The House From Above
days.prepTonight: Tape two big sheets of paper into one and leave it out with the ruler and the crayons. Count the oranges: tomorrow wants six.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Counting the Corners of Every Room

opening.title: Counting the Corners of Every Room
opening.need: the downstairs rooms · 1 sheet of paper · 1 pencil.
steps: Start in the kitchen. She walks the whole edge of the room with one hand flat on the wall until she is back where she began.
Count the corners out loud as her hand turns each one, and put that many pencil strokes on the paper. Four in most rooms, more wherever a chimney or a closet sticks in.
Two more rooms the same way, counting the doorways as well as the corners. Tell her the whole downstairs goes onto one sheet at quarter past nine.

main.title: Every Room Is a Shape
materials: 1 large sheet of paper, or two sheets taped together
Small stickers or torn paper squares for the furniture
Masking tape to hold the paper down
steps: Tape the sheet to the table at all four corners so it cannot travel while she leans on it.

Draw the downstairs from above with the pencil and ruler while she watches. Plain rectangles, one per room, sharing their walls. No windows, no detail. Say out loud that this whole sheet is the one box marked home on the town map she drew two weeks ago.
Ask which room is which and correct nothing. If she calls the kitchen the sitting room, put your finger on the doorway and walk it across the paper.
Give her a color per room and let her fill one in at a time, saying the room name as she starts.
Stop after every room and walk into it together. Stand in the middle, come back, and let her find it on the paper.
Stick a sticker or a torn paper square where the sofa is, where the table is, where the front door lets you in.
main.tip: The coloring keeps her at the table long enough to do the walking six times.

outside.title: Finding the Rooms From Outside
paras: Roll the plan up, carry it out and stand where you can see the whole front of the house. Every room she colored in is behind that wall, and she has never once had to think about it. Ask her where the kitchen is from out here and let her point at the brick rather than the paper. Walk round to the back if you can get there and ask again, because her answer has to change and the house does not. Finish on the front door, the one thing that is on the paper and in front of her at the same time.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and walks through the middle of whatever is happening, so the plan travels rolled up rather than spread on the ground. He points at pictures in books now, so hold him facing the house, put his finger on the real front door and then on the drawn one, and say the word both times.

second.title: The X on the Map
second.intro: Hiding something and marking the spot turns her drawing into a set of instructions.
materials: A cushion or a dish towel to hide them under
steps: Give her a job out of the room: counting to twenty at the top of the stairs.
Hide one toy under the cushion or the dish towel in a room she colored in. Somewhere obvious the first time.
Bring her back and draw a red X on the map, on the room where the toy is. Do not say the room name.
She goes and looks. If she is stuck, put her finger on the X and walk it off the edge of the paper towards the door.
Swap over. She hides one and draws the X, and her X lands in the wrong room for the first two goes.
Once she has it, hide two at a time and mark both. She has to read the map twice.
Finish by hiding one in the hall or on the stairs, somewhere with no room of its own, and let her tell you the map is wrong. She is right.
second.tip: Draw the X while she is watching. Seeing the mark go down ties the paper to the room.

alternatives: Hide things and give directions out loud instead.
Draw the upstairs and tape it above the downstairs.
Build the map in blocks, one block per room.
Chalk a trail of arrows to something in the yard.
outAgain: Feeding the ducks, with oats or defrosted peas, never bread
The long way round to the water, past the turning trees
A playground you have not been to, found on the phone map first
The riverside path, looking down from the bridge
Home for an early bath, if Sunday has run out
days.krestonPM: At the water he is 15 months and running, so this afternoon needs a hand on him from the car to the bench. Give him his own pot of oats to hold and tip out, because tipping is what he works at with a spoon at every meal. He will feed his own feet as much as the ducks.

insight.headline: A map is an abstraction she has to be taught to read.
paras: A map is a picture of a place, taken from a position nobody has ever stood in, drawn at a size the place is not. Azlyn has no reason to find that obvious. Walking the walls this morning put the shape of each room in her legs, and stopping after every one to go and stand in it gave her the link. Around three, children start matching a simple map to a real room, and the ones who manage it have been shown the correspondence rather than told about it. Point at the paper, then point at the wall. Do that six times and the paper starts to mean the room.

days.safety: Reading the front of the house puts all three of you out on the sidewalk. Stand on the house side of the walk, keep yourself between the two of them and the road, and hold Kreston's hand from the front door onward or leave him in the stroller with the brake on. She points from where she is standing and does not step back into the street for a better view. At the pond this afternoon he stays within arm's reach of you the whole time, water in sight or not.

days.title: The Plate That Looks Like a Tile
days.prepTonight: Stand the biggest tray in the house on the counter with the cinnamon, and check the fridge drawer holds six oranges, a cucumber and two carrots.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Colors in the Fridge Drawer

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Long Bath After the Sticky Day

opening.title: The Colors in the Fridge Drawer
opening.need: the fridge drawer · 1 large tray · a clear bit of counter she can reach.
steps: Pull the drawer out and set it on the floor. Let her empty it one piece at a time.
Line the food up along the tray on the counter, lightest to darkest, or in color groups if she takes it that way.
Ask what shape each one will be if you cut straight across it. Take the guesses without correcting one, and tell her you find out at 9:15.

main.title: The Tile You Can Eat
materials: 1 large tray or the biggest plate in the house
steps: Do the sharp-knife work first, at your end of the counter: oranges into wheels, carrots into rounds and each round halved into triangles, cheese into squares, pita into triangles.
Hand her the cucumber and the butter knife. It gives under a push and she gets through the whole one.
Run the pita triangles round the edge of the tray as a border, all pointing the same way. She lays them.
Lay the first run of four along the top: orange wheel, cucumber, cheese square, carrot triangle. Start the second run and let her carry on.
When the order breaks, put your finger on the last correct piece and name the next one.
Dust cinnamon over the orange wheels and slide the tray into the fridge. It comes out at 1:00 for the low table, so keep lunch light and tell her the pattern has to hold until then.
main.tip: Keep the run four pieces long. Three is too few to feel like a rule, and five is more than she can hold while she digs for a carrot.

outside.title: The Last of the Blackberries
paras: Late September is the last of the blackberries, and only if you are far enough north to still have any. Walk to the roughest hedge you can reach, a field edge or the back of the park. Take the ones that come away in her fingers and leave the red ones. She carries more than she eats, because none of it gets eaten until it is washed at home. Look at one bramble: green fruit, red fruit and black fruit on the same stem.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and spoons his own food, so he gets blackberries in a pot at home, washed first and squashed with a fork before they go near him. He runs into the hedge given half a chance and brambles sit at his face height. Carry him past the thorny stretch and put him down on the path.

second.title: The Table on the Floor
second.intro: The morning's tray comes out of the fridge onto a table low enough for Azlyn to reach the middle of, and everybody eats on the floor round it.
materials: This morning's tray, out of the fridge
The coffee table, or a box turned upside down
Cushions or folded blankets, one per person
Fresh mint if you have it, a squeeze of lemon if you do not
steps: Push the coffee table into the middle of the room, or stand a box upside down in its place. Let her pick the room.
Lay a cushion or a folded blanket for every person in the house, and let her place them.
Peel the four oranges with her. Thumbs in at the top, peel off in pieces, and she is better by the fourth.
Lay a peeled orange on its side and let her saw it into wheels with the butter knife. The juice is half the appeal.
Fan the wheels round the serving plate, dust cinnamon across them, tear the mint over the top. Lemon does the same job.
Tear the flatbread instead of cutting it, one piece per person, into the middle where everybody reaches.
Carry the tray out last, set it in the middle beside the oranges, and sit down to eat. No chairs, no plate each, everything from the middle.
second.tip: She can get up and come back without asking, and she comes back more than from a chair.

alternatives: Orange wheels and cinnamon, eaten standing in the kitchen.
Cut everything into circles and count them.
A picnic blanket instead of the low table.
Peel two oranges and count the segments into piles.
outAgain: The field walk, stubble cut and open right up to the hedge
The blackberry lane again, with a tub
The park, for running off a heavy lunch
The green space with a ball, while the light holds
The garden, picking the last of whatever is out there
days.krestonPM: He gets his own cushion at the low table and he will stand on it. At 15 months he spoons his own food and manages orange in his fingers. His portion goes on quartered lengthways, because an orange wheel is a circle of the one wrong size. Out in the field, cut stubble is hard on knees.

insight.headline: Food is the most memorable route into a culture at this age.
paras: Azlyn will not hold on to the word zellij. She will hold on to sitting on the floor round a low table eating orange with cinnamon on it, and the next time Morocco turns up in her life that memory is waiting for it. Taste and smell attach to memory harder than anything she sees or hears, which is why a food eaten once at three comes back at thirty. The tray taught her the pattern. Eating off the floor round a low table told her other people arrange a meal another way and it works fine. Cook the thing rather than explaining the country.

days.safety: Azlyn gets the butter knife and you keep the sharp one, put down behind you between cuts and never left near the counter edge. Kreston is 15 months and spoons his own food now, so his portion goes on quartered lengthways: no whole grapes, no round orange wheels. Wash the blackberries and pick above dog height.

days.title: Folded in Half
days.prepTonight: Dye tomorrow's pasta: penne in three bags, a splash of vinegar and food coloring in each, shaken hard and spread out to dry. Paper and scissors on the table for the morning.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Shape That Comes Out Twice

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Leaves That Fold in Half

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Two Books and the Landing Light

opening.title: One Fold, Two Halves
opening.need: plain paper, 4 or 5 sheets · 1 pencil · crayons.
steps: Fold one sheet in half, let her press the crease flat with her thumbnail, then open it out and show her the two halves.
Draw a wobbly line down your side of the crease with the pencil and ask her to copy it. She cannot.
Let her fold three or four more sheets and color one half of each with the crayons, leaving the other half blank.

main.title: The Shape That Comes Out Twice
materials: A tray or shallow box to catch the scraps
steps: Fold a sheet in half and hold it crease towards her. Draw half a heart on the folded edge with the pencil, the flat side against the crease.
Cut along the line yourself with the adult scissors, then hand it over and let her open it. A whole heart, and she did not see it coming.
Fold the next one and let her draw on it. Anything she likes, as long as it touches the crease. She cuts this one with the child-safe pair while you hold the fold shut.
Keep going. Ten sheets, twelve. Half a circle makes a circle. Half a person makes a person. Half of nothing makes a butterfly.
Cut one with the shape nowhere near the crease, so it opens into two loose halves that join nothing. Let her put the difference into her own words.
Color the openings in with the crayons, both sides matching, and tip the scraps into the tray.
main.tip: Say nothing about symmetry. The word can arrive any time in the next two years.

outside.title: The Leaves That Fold in Half
paras: Take a bag out, collect leaves, then sit on a wall and fold each one along its middle rib. Some meet edge to edge. A linden or a beech shuts like a book. A horse chestnut leaflet is close and off by a bit. Let her sort them into a pile that folds and a pile that does not, and hold your tongue about the wrong ones.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and tears every leaf he is handed, so give him the rejects. Tearing is a two-handed job with each hand doing the opposite of the other, and he has only had it a few weeks. He points at the pile and wants another one. Let him work through as many as you can pick.

second.title: Folding the Laundry in Half
second.intro: The clean laundry comes out of the basket onto the living room floor, all of it at once, and she does the folding.
materials: A basket or bag per bedroom
steps: Tip the whole basket out on the floor space you cleared and sit down in it with her. A pile that size is most of the appeal.
Sort into color piles first. Whites, darks, everything else. She will argue about a gray one, and it goes wherever she says.
Show her one fold on a dish towel: edge to edge, press the crease. Let her do the next six.
Hand her the flat things only. Dish towels, washcloths, her own T-shirts. Sleeves and pant legs are next year.
Pair the socks, two of a kind folded over each other. Clip the ones with no partner and hang the clothespins off the basket handle.
Load a basket or a bag for each bedroom and let her carry them up one at a time.
Put her own pile into her own drawer, and let her put it in crooked.
second.tip: Her folds are not going to be good. Fold hers again if it bothers you, and do it after bedtime.

alternatives: Cut folded paper snowflakes and stop there.
Fold and cut a chain of paper people holding hands.
Sort the socks and skip everything else in the basket.
Fold paper into fans and tape three into a wheel.
outAgain: Swimming
Indoor playground, if a school has the pool this afternoon
The park with a change of clothes, if the water is out
The rec center café, for anyone who has had enough
Home, if the laundry is still on the floor
days.krestonPM: He comes to the pool at 15 months, and he walks the tiles now. Hold him from the changing room to the water. In the pool he steps down off the top step into your hands, over and over, and twenty minutes is plenty.

insight.headline: Symmetry through folding is discovered, not explained.
paras: You could tell Azlyn that a butterfly has matching sides. Folding a sheet, cutting once and opening it puts the fact in her hands, and her face at the moment it opens is the argument for doing it that way. Children who work through a physical version of a rule hold on to it far longer than children who get told the rule, because the folding builds the idea out of a movement she made herself. She will find halves everywhere for about a week: her plate, her face in the mirror, a leaf. Go round after her and name what she finds.

days.safety: The adult scissors stay with you and go back in your pocket between cuts, not on the floor. The child-safe pair comes back to you every time she puts it down. Kreston runs now and paper scraps go straight in his mouth, so the tray catches them and the floor gets swept before he is loose. At the pool he is within arm's reach the whole time.

days.title: The Border Round the Room
days.prepTonight: Tape eight to ten sheets end to end into one long strip and roll it up, spread newspaper down the table, check the dyed pasta has dried.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Border That Goes All the Way Round

opening.title: Three Stamps Before Breakfast
opening.need: 2 potatoes · 1 kitchen sponge · 1 sharp knife (adult only) · 3 saucers · poster paint in 3 colors · newspaper.
steps: Halve two potatoes and carve a square into one flat face, a triangle into another, and cut a circle out of the sponge. The cutting is yours.
Put the knife away out of reach. Squeeze a blob of paint onto each saucer and let her spread it flat with a finger.
Print one of each shape onto the newspaper.

main.title: The Border That Goes All the Way Round
materials: 1 long strip of paper, butcher paper or 8–10 sheets taped end to end
2 potatoes cut into a square and a triangle, adult only
1 kitchen sponge cut into a circle
An old shirt or an apron
steps: Lay newspaper down the table and unroll the strip on top. Tape both ends down.
Put her in the old shirt or the apron, sleeves pushed back. She leans on this one.
Set the saucers out in the order the pattern runs: blue for the potato square, red for the potato triangle, yellow for the sponge circle. Each stamp stays in its saucer.
Print the three at the start of the strip, say the order out loud, and hand her the square again.
Let her run the strip. Say the order under your breath and stop once she keeps going without you.
Wipe her hands on the damp washcloth, leave the strip to dry, then tape it round the wall at her eye height.
main.tip: Three in a repeating order is harder than red-blue-red-blue, and she will drop back to two without noticing. Let the wrong run stand.

outside.title: Rubbings From the Sidewalk
paras: Take paper and a fat crayon on its side and rub everything flat you pass: a drain cover, a wooden gate, a brick, the stamped date on a paving slab. Hold the paper still while she rubs. The drain cover is the one worth the walk, because most carry a repeating pattern cast into the iron.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and holds a crayon in his fist and drags it. Give him a sheet flat on a paving slab and let him scribble while she works the drain cover. He points at pictures in books now, so hold her rubbing up and put his finger on one of the shapes.

second.title: Three Then Start Again
second.intro: Threading puts the same order into her fingers one piece at a time.
materials: Dried penne or rigatoni, dyed in 3 colors the night before
1 ball of wool or thick string
Sticky tape wrapped round one end of the wool to make a needle
steps: Tip the pasta into three bowls, one color each, set left to right in the order the pattern runs.
Wrap sticky tape tight round the end of the wool until it is a stiff point she can push through a tube.
Cut an arm's length off the ball, put the ball away, and tie a fat knot in the far end so the pasta stops there.
Thread one of each color yourself, then hand it over. Say the next color when she asks and stop once she stops asking.
When the order breaks, hold the string up by the taped end and run her finger down it until she finds where the rule stopped.
Fill the arm's length, tie the ends together and let her wear it, or hang it under the strip.
Count the pasta back into the bowls, out loud, and put them up high.
second.tip: She finds her own mistakes long before she can fix them. Hang the wrong string up anyway.

alternatives: Thread two colors, and go to three when she has it.
Lay the pasta in a line without threading it.
Print a second strip for her bedroom door.
Sort the pasta back into color bowls.
outAgain: The church hall playgroup, and take the pasta string to show
Indoor playground, if the hall is shut this week
The library on the way home, for something long enough for tonight
The park while the strip dries
The store for milk, and let her carry it home
days.krestonPM: At playgroup he is 15 months and running. He heads for the older children and stands at the edge of them watching. Let him take one thing off the toy shelf and carry it round the hall, because carrying while walking is new.

insight.headline: Repeating units are a genuine step up from alternating patterns.
paras: Azlyn has been doing red-blue-red-blue since she was two, and it works because she only has to remember the last thing she put down. A run of three is a different job. She has to hold the whole unit in her head, know where in it she is standing, and know that the end of it sends her back to the beginning. Pattern work at three sits alongside early number knowledge as one of the things that shows up later in her math, and the unit of three is where it starts to bite. She will drop back to two when she is tired, and that is information rather than failure.

days.safety: The knife that cuts the potato stamps is adult-only and goes out of reach the moment the last shape is carved. Wet paint on a hard floor is slippery, so the newspaper goes down first and spills get wiped as they happen. Dyed pasta is the size Kreston chokes on at 15 months. It stays on the table and gets counted back into the bowls before he is down. The wool comes off the ball at an arm's length and the rest goes away. A worn string stays on only while you are beside her and comes off before she leaves the table, and the finished one hangs out of reach rather than over a chair back. A loop of string at toddler height is a strangulation risk, and a serious one.

days.title: The Pattern You Sweep Up
days.prepTonight: Stand the basket and her rain boots by the back door with the chalk box, and put the broom somewhere she can reach it.

schedule.name: Bath and the Dark Coming Earlier

opening.title: Gathering the Loose Color
opening.need: 1 basket · the yard, the path and whatever hedge you can reach · her rain boots.
steps: Rain boots on and straight out with the basket, no plan past filling it. Leaves, petals, small stones, buckeyes, seed heads, whatever came down overnight.
Group it on the doorstep by color rather than by what it is. Brown leaves with brown buckeyes, red with red.
Ask which color there is most of, count the biggest pile, and leave the lot on the step.

main.title: The Circle on the Path
materials: A basket of leaves, petals, small stones, buckeyes and seed heads
Dried pasta and jar lids to fill the gaps
steps: Chalk a small circle on the path, then three or four rings round it, each a hand's width out from the last. Let her hold the chalk for the outer ones.
Fill the middle circle first with one material and nothing else, packed tight. Buckeyes, or the reddest leaves.
Work outward a ring at a time, changing color at each one. She decides what goes where and you fetch and carry.
When a ring runs short, fill the gap with pasta or jar lids instead of going out for more.
Stand back on the step and look at the whole thing from above.
Photograph it on your phone once she says it is done.
main.tip: Hand her the soft broom and the bucket at the end and let her sweep her own circle into it.

outside.title: Green to Red Along the Wall
paras: Today the day and the night run the same length, and from tomorrow the dark takes more of it every week until the shortest day, a few days before Christmas. Say so out loud while you walk. Find a wall with something climbing it: Virginia creeper, ivy, an old bramble. The color runs along it, green at the shaded end and red where the sun hits. Let her tell you where green turns into red. The change has no edge, and she will hunt for one.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and walks straight through anything laid out on a path, which is why the circle gets photographed early. At the wall he stays in your arms and looks, because everything growing on it is out of bounds for him. Hand him a leaf out of the basket instead and take it back before it reaches his mouth.

second.title: Washing It Off With a Bucket
second.intro: Chalk on a patio comes off with water, and the pouring is the part she will still be talking about at bedtime.
materials: 1 old towel by the back door
steps: Rain boots on before she goes out. This afternoon soaks the ground, and her socks stay dry or the whole thing ends early.
Give her the full box of chalk and the run of the patio. Big shapes, whole slabs filled in, a color per slab.
Let her run yesterday's order across the slabs: square, triangle, circle, then start again. Two rows is plenty.
Stand back and look at it with her. Ask whether she wants to keep it, and take the answer she gives.
Carry the bucket of warm water out and let her tip it over one end of the pattern, with your hand on the handle beside hers.
She scrubs with the sponge and the dish brush and watches the color run down into the drain. Chalk goes cloudy in water and she will follow the cloud.
Tip the last of it out, stand the bucket upside down against the wall, and dry her on the old towel.
second.tip: Let her be the one who pours. It sits better when her own hands did it.

alternatives: Chalk the path and leave it for the rain.
Lay the circle indoors on a tray and photograph it.
Wash the front step and the trash cans with the bucket.
Sort the basket back into colors for the birds.
outAgain: The thrift store, with a dollar of her own for whatever she picks
The bakery on the way back, eaten on the wall outside
The park, for the last of the light, which goes at seven now
The woods loop, kicking through what has come down
A drive out to a view of the sunset
days.krestonPM: In the thrift store he is 15 months and he runs to the toy shelf and stays there. Let him. Half the toys are missing pieces and all of them are cheap, so buy whatever he carries to the register. He points at pictures in books now, and the book box is fifty cents.

insight.headline: Impermanence is easier to accept when it's built into the design.
paras: Nothing on the path this morning was glued down, and Azlyn knew that before she started. A thing built to be swept up gets grieved over less than a thing she thought would last, because the ending was part of the deal she agreed to at the beginning. She still got the making of it, the photograph, and the sweeping, which plenty of children enjoy more than the building. Sand mandalas, chalk drawings and pastry run on the same terms. Say at the start that it comes down at the end, name who will be doing the sweeping, then hold to both halves of it.

days.safety: Kreston is 15 months and walks through anything laid out on the floor, which is half the design today, and buckeyes, acorns, small stones and dried pasta all go in his mouth first. He stays on the step or in your arms while the rings go down, the circle gets photographed before he is put down, and the path is swept into the bucket before he walks it. Ivy and Virginia creeper are both poisonous and the bramble carries thorns at his face height, so nothing comes off that wall into his hands. He watches it from your arms. A child his age can drown in a few inches of water, so the bucket stays beside you and gets tipped out the second you have finished.
